BODY:
A vintage Gibson Les Paul Junior with its original sunburst finish falls within the site's $6,000 to $13,000 reference for 1954 to 1958 single-cutaway guitars. The corresponding single-cutaway TV Model reference is $10,000 to $20,000. I start with the body style and finish, then narrow the comparison around the pickup, repairs, wear and case.

This page covers the earlier slab-body Junior and its one-pickup TV counterpart. For serials, parts and construction evidence, use my [Les Paul Junior dating and authentication guide](/post/gibson-les-paul-junior-guide/). A guitar with the later pointed SG body belongs in a separate comparison, even when its headstock still says Les Paul Junior.

## Gibson Les Paul Junior Values By Year

These references were reviewed as of October 2026. The single-cutaway ranges preserve the figures already published in my Les Paul market guide. The cherry double-cutaway range comes from the 2025 Official Vintage Guitar Magazine Price Guide, with completed Reverb transactions used to check the difference between worn instruments and the book's excellent-condition category.

The table assumes an all-original guitar in excellent condition with its original case. A quality refret preserves the all-original classification of an otherwise all-original guitar, although it takes it out of the museum-quality category. Missing cases, replacement parts, refinishing and structural repairs require a separate appraisal.

| Year | Configuration | Reference Range | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1954 | Single-cutaway sunburst | $6,000 to $13,000 | 1954 to 1958 shared site reference |
| 1955 | Single-cutaway sunburst | $6,000 to $13,000 | 1954 to 1958 shared site reference |
| 1955 | Single-cutaway TV Model | $10,000 to $20,000 | 1955 to 1958 shared site reference |
| 1956 | Single-cutaway sunburst | $6,000 to $13,000 | 1954 to 1958 shared site reference |
| 1956 | Single-cutaway TV Model | $10,000 to $20,000 | 1955 to 1958 shared site reference |
| 1957 | Single-cutaway sunburst | $6,000 to $13,000 | 1954 to 1958 shared site reference |
| 1957 | Single-cutaway TV Model | $10,000 to $20,000 | 1955 to 1958 shared site reference |
| 1958 | Single-cutaway sunburst | $6,000 to $13,000 | 1954 to 1958 shared site reference |
| 1958 | Single-cutaway TV Model | $10,000 to $20,000 | 1955 to 1958 shared site reference |
| 1958 | Rounded double-cutaway cherry | $10,500 to $13,500 | 1958 to 1960 shared published clean-condition reference |
| 1959 | Rounded double-cutaway cherry | $10,500 to $13,500 | 1958 to 1960 shared published clean-condition reference |
| 1960 | Rounded double-cutaway cherry | $10,500 to $13,500 | 1958 to 1960 shared published clean-condition reference |

Each repeated range is a shared configuration reference. It doesn't mean I found a different completed sale sample for every year or that every guitar from an era deserves the same price. The two 1958 body styles appear separately because the shape changes the comparison.

The double-cutaway evidence needs that distinction between condition categories. The completed cherry examples checked for this guide were described as Very Good and sold below the excellent-condition book range. One retained its original case; the other had a bent tuner and no established case inventory. I haven't promoted those descriptions into proof of pristine condition.

The 2025 book also places clean single-cutaway sunburst and TV instruments above parts of the site's existing ranges. I've retained the published site figures here. Those differences are a reason to inspect a particular guitar and compare its condition, not a basis for quietly raising every annual row.

[IMAGE 1]

## Match The Body Style Before Comparing Prices

The Junior has one pickup, but the name covers more than one guitar. The original single-cutaway body, the later rounded double-cutaway body and the pointed SG body need separate comparisons. A listing that says only “vintage Les Paul Junior” leaves out information I'd need before valuing it.

For this table, single-cutaway means one opening beside the neck. The rounded double-cutaway has an opening on each side and a slab body. The later SG has pointed horns and a thinner, contoured shape. Those broad distinctions are enough to choose a pricing family; the detailed year and component checks belong in the authentication guide.

### Single-Cutaway Sunburst

The 1954 to 1958 sunburst reference covers the familiar flat mahogany body with one black P-90 pickup and a wraparound bridge. A P-90 is the pickup design; “dog ear” describes the cover's mounting tabs. The bridge also anchors the strings, so there's no separate tailpiece behind it.

Within the shared range, I'd compare a clean instrument with another clean instrument before making allowances for wear or changed parts. The finish, pickup and intact body belong in that comparison together. A replacement bridge on an otherwise original guitar is a different question from a replaced pickup and an enlarged pickup cavity.

The first production year doesn't automatically supply a fixed premium. Neither does a seller's description of a particularly large neck. A guitar's year helps establish the group, but condition and retained components determine where it can sit within it.

### Rounded Double-Cutaway Cherry

The rounded double-cutaway became part of the Junior line in 1958. Cherry is the configuration covered by the additional reference in this guide. An unusual finish, a TV example or a guitar with a changed body finish needs its own comparison.

For an excellent, all-original cherry example with its original case, the published-reference band is $10,500 to $13,500. The recent worn examples used as a check show why that clean category shouldn't be applied automatically to every double-cut Junior. I'd also separate an undamaged guitar from one with a repaired neck or altered pickup mounting.

The table stops its rounded double-cutaway rows at 1960, matching the main production sequence in my existing model guide. A guitar represented as a 1961 rounded double-cutaway needs its actual configuration assessed. I wouldn't turn a disputed transition label into a separate annual price premium.

[IMAGE 2]

### Les Paul Branding On An SG Body

Early SG-shaped Juniors can still carry Les Paul Junior lettering. The lettering doesn't make them equivalent to the earlier slab-body guitars in this table. Compare them using the [Gibson SG Junior value guide](/vintage-gibson-sg-junior-value-guide/), which follows the later model's production years.

That distinction also keeps a 1960s guitar from being valued against a 1950s sunburst simply because both have one pickup. I don't extend the earlier slab-body table through the 1970s where that configuration wasn't the production model. Later reissues require another comparison again.

## What TV Yellow Changes

The one-pickup Les Paul TV Model shares the Junior's basic role, but its finish and model identity create a separate collector comparison. For the 1955 to 1958 single-cutaway examples covered here, the site's existing reference is $10,000 to $20,000. The range assumes original finish and the condition stated above.

TV Yellow doesn't mean every pale Gibson has the same value. The one-pickup TV Model and the two-pickup Les Paul Special are different models. My [Les Paul TV Model guide](/post/gibson-les-paul-tv-model-guide/) covers that identity, while the [single-cutaway Les Paul Special guide](/post/1955-1958-tv-yellow-les-paul-special-guide/) shows the two-pickup instrument.

A refinished sunburst Junior doesn't acquire the original TV Model comparison because somebody painted it yellow. I'd retain its actual identity in the appraisal and describe the finish work. A color can be attractive to a player without supplying the history a collector is paying for.

The fretboard dots on the Junior and TV Model are cream-colored celluloid dot inlays. I wouldn't describe them as pearl or use a supposed change from pearl to plastic to justify a year premium. The ordinary appointments are part of these student models' identity.

[IMAGE 3]

The table's TV range is confined to the single-cutaway configuration. It isn't a price for every later rounded or SG-shaped TV guitar. I haven't supplied a double-cutaway TV band from dealer advertisements alone.

## Original Parts And Repairs Move The Comparison

A Junior's short parts list makes a description like “mostly original” too vague to price. I need to know which part changed, what work accompanied the change and whether the removed original survives. The same phrase can describe a replaced strap button or a different pickup installed after wood was removed.

An appraisal should account for the whole guitar. Adding separate deductions for the same underlying alteration can count the damage twice. A refinished neck repair, for example, needs one assessment of the repair, refinishing and remaining original material together.

### The Pickup And Its Mounting

The Junior's single pickup does the electrical work for the whole instrument. An original pickup, a rewound original and a modern replacement need to be described separately. A working pickup alone doesn't settle its history.

I also distinguish a reversible component change from altered wood. A replacement cover or mounting screw can be addressed differently from a pickup cavity enlarged for another design. Returning a P-90 to an altered cavity doesn't put the removed wood back.

Keep any removed pickup, cover or hardware with the guitar. I can assess what survives before you decide to reinstall anything. A bag of loose parts needs its own review; it doesn't automatically prove that every part left the factory on that instrument.

### The Bridge And Tuners

The wraparound bridge affects the playing setup as well as the collector description. I want to know if a later bridge was fitted, if the original is included and if its mounting was changed. The answer can differ from a guitar that simply needs an ordinary setup.

Tuners need the same distinction. A working replacement set with no further alteration is a different case from enlarged holes or additional screw holes. Reinstalling old-looking machines doesn't erase earlier modifications.

[IMAGE 4]

### Neck Repairs And Fretwork

A repaired headstock or neck joint moves the guitar out of the clean, unrepaired table category. I need clear photographs of the repair and any available work records before choosing a comparison. The location, extent and present condition of the work affect the appraisal.

A quality refret is accepted maintenance and preserves the all-original classification of an otherwise all-original guitar. It does mean the guitar is no longer museum quality. I keep that separate from neck reshaping, a replaced fingerboard or other changes to the wood.

If the guitar plays badly, that doesn't establish that it needs a refret or a structural repair. Have the problem identified before approving work. For an initial valuation, photographs and a description of the symptoms are more useful than a guess about what a repair shop might charge.

## Wear, Refinishing And The Top Of The Range

Original finish with visible playing wear belongs in a different comparison from fresh replacement lacquer. A glossy guitar can have extensive work beneath that appearance. I don't choose the clean-original price bracket from shine alone.

The same applies to faded cherry. Color saturation is one visible characteristic, while originality, condition and repairs remain separate questions. A bright color doesn't establish an untouched finish, and fading by itself doesn't tell me the guitar's complete history.

I use the highest part of a clean range only when the guitar supports it. The case, retained parts, structural condition and finish all need to fit the comparison. Calling an instrument “collector grade” in an advertisement supplies none of that evidence by itself.

A modified Junior can still suit a player very well. That doesn't make the work disappear from its collector description. An accurate account of the modifications gives both sides a usable basis for discussing its price.

### Why I Don't Apply One Refinish Percentage

The effect of refinishing depends on what else remains. An otherwise intact Junior with documented finish work is different from a routed guitar with a replaced pickup, changed bridge and neck repair. One percentage would conceal those differences.

The same problem appears when several generic discounts are added together. A guide can identify the direction of the change, but the modified guitar needs comparable modified instruments. The clean table gives me a reference category, not a formula for every possible repair combination.

## The Case And Paperwork Belong With The Guitar

The case is part of the condition assumption in the table. If it's missing, replaced or damaged, say so before comparing a guitar with a complete example. I don't treat a modern protective case as equivalent to the original case for collector purposes.

A surviving original case doesn't have to be suitable for shipping. Its collector role and its ability to protect the instrument in transit are separate questions. Keep it with the guitar while planning transport around the instrument's actual support and protection needs.

[IMAGE 5]

Receipts, old photographs and repair records can help establish a guitar's history. They don't replace an examination of the instrument. I compare what the records show with the guitar as it exists today.

An old photograph may document a finish or show that a particular alteration was already present. It may also be too distant to establish any specific part. I don't convert an unclear family photograph into a claim that the guitar has never been changed.

Keep the records together, including notes about work you know was done. You don't need a continuous ownership history before requesting an appraisal. An honest account of what you know and what remains uncertain is enough to start.

## Read Sale Comparisons On The Same Terms

A completed sale records an outcome; an asking price records a seller's request. I keep those categories separate. An unsold advertisement at the top of a search result doesn't establish the current market for every Junior with a similar appearance.

Condition labels also need the underlying description. “Excellent” can still accompany a disclosed replacement part, while “Very Good” can describe an original guitar with playing wear. I read the repair, finish and case information before deciding how a result applies.

The double-cutaway reference here combines a named 2025 printed guide with two independently checked completed transactions from 2026. The transactions support the market comparison but don't match every condition assumption of the book. That limitation is why the table identifies the band as a published clean-condition reference.

The existing single-cutaway sunburst and TV figures have a different basis: they're retained site anchors. I haven't relabeled them as a new sample of completed sales. The [Les Paul family market guide](/vintage-gibson-les-paul-market-value-guide/) supplies their original context.

### Sale Price, Proceeds And An Offer

The amount a buyer pays and the amount a seller keeps can differ. Fees, shipping, insurance and the agreed terms need to be considered before comparing routes to sale. A private-sale listing and a direct offer also place different responsibilities on the owner.

The table isn't a standing purchase offer. I need the particular guitar's details before discussing what I can offer for it. When comparing offers, include the case and loose parts consistently so you're comparing the same package.

An insurance replacement figure serves a different purpose from a sale estimate. Tell the appraiser which question you need answered. A number prepared for one purpose shouldn't silently become the answer to another.

## Photograph The Guitar Before Changing It

Start with clear photographs of the whole front and back, the headstock from both sides, the bridge and pickup, and any known repair. Include the case and loose parts. Natural light and sharp focus help me see the instrument more clearly than a dark photograph with heavy color correction.

You don't need to take the pickup apart or disturb old wiring for an initial appraisal. If internal photographs are needed, I can explain what would help and discuss having the work done by someone comfortable with vintage instruments. Preserve the guitar's present condition while documenting it.

[IMAGE 6]

Tell me if you know of a refret, finish work, tuner change, pickup repair or neck damage. If you don't know, say that. I won't treat an uncertain family account as a guarantee that nothing has ever changed.

My [free vintage guitar appraisal](/free-appraisal/) is a place to begin with those photographs. I buy vintage Gibsons nationwide from Mesa, Arizona, and can discuss the particular guitar after reviewing what you have.

mainEntity.name: What Is A Vintage Gibson Les Paul Junior Worth?

acceptedAnswer.text: The existing site reference for 1954 to 1958 sunburst single-cutaway Juniors is $6,000 to $13,000. The corresponding 1955 to 1958 single-cutaway TV Model reference is $10,000 to $20,000. These assume an all-original guitar in excellent condition with its original case; repairs and changed parts require a separate comparison.

mainEntity.name: What Is A 1956 Gibson Les Paul Junior Worth?

acceptedAnswer.text: A sunburst 1956 Junior falls within the shared 1954 to 1958 reference of $6,000 to $13,000. A single-cutaway TV Model uses the separate $10,000 to $20,000 reference. I need to confirm the finish, retained parts, condition and case before narrowing either range.

mainEntity.name: What Is A 1959 Cherry Les Paul Junior Worth?

acceptedAnswer.text: The published clean-condition reference used here is $10,500 to $13,500 for a rounded double-cutaway cherry Junior. It's a shared era range from the 2025 Official Vintage Guitar Magazine Price Guide, checked against completed 2026 sales of worn examples. Those sales were below the book range, so it shouldn't be applied automatically to a guitar in Very Good condition.

mainEntity.name: Is A TV Model The Same As A Les Paul Special?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The TV Model discussed here has one pickup and belongs with the Junior comparison. A Les Paul Special has two pickups and needs its own model comparison. TV Yellow alone doesn't establish which model you have.

mainEntity.name: Why Does This Table Stop Before 1979?

acceptedAnswer.text: This table covers the earlier slab-body configuration. Later pointed SG-shaped Juniors belong in the SG Junior value guide, even if they retain Les Paul Junior lettering. I don't extend an earlier body's price range into years when a different configuration was the production model.

mainEntity.name: Does A Quality Refret Make A Junior Non-Original?

acceptedAnswer.text: A quality refret is accepted maintenance and preserves the all-original classification of an otherwise all-original guitar. It takes the guitar out of the museum-quality category. Neck reshaping and a replaced fingerboard are separate alterations.

mainEntity.name: Does A Refinish Have A Fixed Percentage Deduction?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. I assess the finish work together with the guitar's remaining original parts and any structural repairs. A single percentage can conceal the differences between an otherwise intact guitar and a heavily modified one.

mainEntity.name: Should I Replace Parts Before Asking For An Appraisal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Document the guitar as it is and keep any removed original parts with it. I don't need you to reinstall hardware, disturb wiring or authorize cosmetic work before an initial appraisal. Clear photographs and the repair history you know are enough to start.

STRIP_INSTRUCTIONS.remove: The Junior exists because Gibson had a price problem in 1954. The cheapest solidbody electric in the catalog was the Les Paul Goldtop at $225 list. Federal minimum wage at the time was 75 cents an hour. A teenager working a summer job could expect to save maybe forty or fifty dollars across the whole season, nowhere near enough to walk out of a music store with a Gibson solidbody. The Korean War had ended the year before, the economy was expanding, and electric guitar sales were climbing fast on the back of country radio and the first rumblings of rock and roll. Gibson needed something it could sell to first-time buyers and music school students, and the existing Les Paul lineup was priced out of that market entirely.

The list price moved up in 1957 from $99.50 to $120. Material costs were climbing and Gibson had started to figure out that working players, not just students, were buying Juniors. The simplicity the catalog framed as a limitation was being treated as a feature by the people actually using these guitars on stage.

Valuation: Understanding What Drives the Market

The vintage Les Paul Junior market is active and well-developed. Specific dollar figures move constantly with market conditions, so this section maps the structural factors that determine where any given Junior sits in the value hierarchy rather than quoting prices that will be wrong by the time you read this. ### Collector Valuation Hierarchy ### The Condition Factor Condition is the single biggest determinant of value within any given configuration. Moving from "good" to "excellent" increases price substantially. Moving from "excellent" to "near mint" can increase price by an equal or greater dollar amount, because pristine vintage Juniors are rare. These were originally student-grade tools, played daily, mostly not stored with care. Survivors in genuinely excellent condition are vastly outnumbered by survivors in honest player condition. ### The Originality Premium Beyond overall condition, the originality of specific components matters significantly. A Junior with all original hardware, electronics, and finish is worth substantially more than one with replaced tuners, a non-original bridge, or replaced pickups, even if the replacements are high-quality period-correct components. Original pickups matter most. The specific sonic character of a vintage P-90 is genuinely difficult to replicate with new-production pickups, even excellent ones, and the market reflects that. ### The Documentation Premium Documented provenance pulls real premiums. Original receipts, owner history, photographs of the instrument at a specific moment in its life. Original cases, hang tags, warranty cards, instruction sheets, any period documentation, all of it adds value. Both for the rarity of the materials themselves and for the authentication support they provide. Bring the case to the deal. Bring the paperwork.

Frequently Asked Questions

Both are P-90 pickups with the same coil construction. They differ in cover design and how they mount. The dog ear, used on the Junior, has extended mounting tabs on its long sides that screw directly into the guitar top. No separate mounting ring needed. The soapbar, used on the Special, Goldtop, and others, has a flush rectangular cover and mounts through a separate frame or directly into the body. The electrical and magnetic specs are essentially identical. Any tonal differences between them come from mounting position and body routing differences, not from the pickup design itself. UV light is your best tool. Small touch-ups show up as localized patches of different fluorescence intensity surrounded by original finish. Full refinishes typically fluoresce uniformly but at a different color or intensity than original 1950s nitro. The areas under hardware (bridge, pickguard, pickup) give you the best comparison points. If those hardware-protected areas match the visible finish exactly, and both differ from what original 1950s nitro should look like under UV, you're probably looking at a full refinish. If the hardware areas show a "ghost" of an older finish while the exposed surfaces look fresh, that points to partial refinish or heavy touch-up. Not automatically, but they need careful evaluation. A well-executed repair, hide glue, properly clamped, no remaining flex or gap at the joint, can be structurally sound for the long term and have minimal effect on tone or playability. A poorly executed repair, or a neck that's been broken and repaired multiple times, may be structurally compromised and at risk of failing again. Have any repaired break evaluated by an experienced luthier before purchase. A verified, clean repair on an otherwise desirable Junior should reduce the asking price, but it doesn't have to eliminate the guitar from consideration. Most experienced players land on the 1958 to 1960 double-cutaway as the best player's Junior. You get the improved upper-fret access, the slab mahogany body and its tonal character, and cleaner authentication compared to the SG era. SG-body 1961 to 1962 examples with well-repaired neck breaks can be excellent players' guitars at lower prices than equivalent double-cutaway examples, but the structural vulnerability of the design requires ongoing awareness and care. Single-cutaway Juniors typically weigh between 7.5 and 9 pounds. Double-cutaways tend to be slightly lighter, 7 to 8.5 pounds. SG-style Juniors are the lightest, usually 6 to 7.5 pounds. Weight does affect tone but the relationship is complex. More mass generally correlates with more sustain and stronger low-frequency body resonance, but the species, age, and density of the specific piece of wood matter more than raw weight. Weight is a useful proxy. It isn't a definitive tonal indicator on its own. Original 1950s Gibsons left the factory with heavy strings by modern standards, .013 to .056 or similar. Running heavy gauges on an aging vintage neck puts ongoing stress on the neck joint, the truss rod, and the body. Most technicians advise vintage owners to drop to lighter gauges, typically .010 to .046 or .011 to .048. You give up a small amount of tone for substantially reduced stress on irreplaceable components. If the guitar is currently set up for a specific gauge, changing significantly will require truss rod adjustment and possibly saddle work to keep the setup right. The Factory Order Number is Gibson's internal production batch code, typically ink-stamped inside the control cavity or visible at the neck joint. FONs were applied when a batch of instruments entered production, and they encode the year and batch sequence in a format that researchers have decoded and published in various reference resources. Cross-referencing the FON against the headstock serial number gives you a more reliable production date range than either number alone. If the two suggest inconsistent dates, that's worth investigating before drawing conclusions about the rest of the instrument.

AUTHENTICATION_FAQ.q: What Pickup Does A Vintage Les Paul Junior Have?
AUTHENTICATION_FAQ.a: The Junior has one P-90 pickup with a dog ear cover. The cover’s projecting mounting tabs distinguish its mounting arrangement from the soapbar cover used on a Les Paul Special.

AUTHENTICATION_FAQ.q: Are The Dot Inlays On A Junior Or TV Model Pearl?
AUTHENTICATION_FAQ.a: No. The Junior and TV Model used cream-colored celluloid dot inlays throughout the original run. A supposed pearl-to-plastic change isn’t a dating feature for these models.

AUTHENTICATION_FAQ.q: Why Does An SG-Shaped Guitar Say Les Paul Junior?
AUTHENTICATION_FAQ.a: Early SG-shaped Juniors retained Les Paul Junior lettering before Gibson dropped the Les Paul name from that line. The body configuration and component evidence need to be assessed together; the lettering alone doesn’t identify the earlier slab-body model.
